The three partitions are blocked by an open transaction. A read_committed consumer only returns records up to the last stable offset, one less than the offset of the first open transaction, so it stops there; the audit consumer (read_uncommitted) is not limited and reads to the end. The killed ledger-writer pod most likely left a transaction open on those partitions. reference: The new consumer rebalance protocol moved the session timeout to the broker. The client's session.timeout.ms is not supported when group.protocol is consumer, so your 120000 is ignored. The group uses the broker's group.consumer.session.timeout.ms, 45 seconds by default, and a 70-second GC pause gets members fenced. You can set it per group with the group config consumer.session.timeout.ms, but it must lie within the broker's minimum and maximum, and group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms defaults to 60000. The order is therefore: first raise group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms (for example to 120000) in spec.kafka.config of the Kafka resource; it is a read-only broker setting, so it takes effect after the rolling restart Strimzi performs. Then run kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server <bootstrap> --alter --entity-type groups --entity-name risk-scoring --add-config consumer.session.timeout.ms=90000. Verify with --describe on the group and watch the next nightly reload. If you would rather not touch the brokers, move the group back to the classic protocol with the documented downgrade; your client setting then works again. Shorter GC pauses would help either way.

Compaction keeps only the latest value per key, so once the cleaner processes the segments, the older values are gone; the tombstone itself stays for delete.retention.ms (1 day by default) so consumers can see the delete, and is then removed. Two settings decide whether that happens within 30 days. First, the active segment is never compacted. With few writes per partition and segment.ms at its default of 7 days, a value can sit in the active segment for a week before it is even eligible. Second, max.compaction.lag.ms sets the longest time a record may stay uncompacted; set it well under 30 days, for example 7 days, which also forces segments to roll. Your controllers do not set it, so the cluster-level default became 1. Kafka's precedence order puts a dynamic cluster-wide default above static broker configuration, so every broker uses 1, and acks=all succeeds with a single in-sync replica. That is what your acceptance test showed. When a KafkaNodePool sets jvmOptions, those take precedence over the Kafka resource's jvmOptions, and the pool's block replaces the Kafka-level block rather than merging with it. Your brokers pool sets only gcLoggingEnabled: false, so the brokers run without -Xms or -Xmx and the Cluster Operator applies its default heap for Kafka: 50% of the memory limit, capped at 5 GB. That matches the smaller heap you see. Fix it by putting -Xms: 6g and -Xmx: 6g in the brokers pool's jvmOptions next to gcLoggingEnabled: false, or move gcLoggingEnabled to the Kafka resource and remove the pool's jvmOptions so the Kafka-level block applies. A 6g heap within a 16Gi limit is reasonable: Kafka relies on the page cache, so leave most of the memory outside the heap. The change rolls the pods; verify the heap afterwards in your JVM metrics.
